title: What is Write-Ahead Logging (WAL): changes are appended to a log and fsync'd BEFORE the data pages are updated, giving durability (replay the log on crash) and enabling point-in-time recovery and replication: and how does it shape a ledger database's backup strategy (a base backup + archived WAL segments lets you restore to any moment)?
shortTitle: Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) and how it shapes a ledger backup strategy
keyPoints: WAL writes every change to a sequential log and fsyncs it to disk BEFORE modifying the actual data pages, decoupling durability from random page writes.
On crash, PostgreSQL replays the WAL from the last checkpoint forward, redoing committed changes and discarding uncommitted ones.
Streaming replication ships WAL records continuously to replicas, which apply them to stay in sync with the primary.
Point-in-time recovery (PITR) restores a base backup and replays archived WAL segments up to any chosen timestamp.
A ledger backup strategy uses periodic base backups plus continuous WAL archiving to durable storage like S3, giving essentially zero committed-data loss.
Checkpoints bound how much WAL must be replayed on recovery; more frequent checkpoints mean faster recovery but more write amplification.
WAL archiving must itself be durable and monitored, because a gap in archived segments breaks the point-in-time recovery chain.

s1_definition.oneliner: Log the change durably first, update the data pages after: so a crash is recovered by replaying the log, and archived logs plus a base backup let you restore to any moment.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)** – A durability protocol where every change is first appended to a sequential log and flushed to disk (fsync) BEFORE the corresponding data pages are modified.
- **Crash recovery** – On restart after a crash, the database replays the WAL from the last checkpoint, redoing committed transactions and discarding uncommitted ones.
- **Replication** – A replica is another server replaying the same WAL stream, staying in sync via streaming replication.
- **Point-in-time recovery** – A base backup plus archived WAL segments lets you restore to any chosen timestamp, not just last night's snapshot.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, before a clerk changes any balance in the big ledger, they first write the exact instruction: 'debit SAV2001 by 50,000' into a sequential diary and make sure the ink is dry (fsync). Only then do they update the ledger page. If the power fails mid-update, the bank reopens the diary and re-applies every instruction that was written down, so no committed transaction is ever lost and the ledger is reconstructed exactly.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)                    │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                            │
│  Transaction: Transfer 50,000 from SAV2001 to SAV2002    │
│                                                            │
│  Step 1: Write WAL records (sequential, fast)             │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐          │
│  │ WAL: [debit SAV2001 -50000] [credit +50000] │          │
│  │ WAL: [COMMIT]                                │          │
│  │ → fsync to disk (durable!)                   │          │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘          │
│                                                            │
│  Step 2: Return COMMIT to application                     │
│                                                            │
│  Step 3: Data pages updated LATER (background)            │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐          │
│  │ Checkpointer flushes dirty pages to disk    │          │
│  │ (happens asynchronously, not blocking)       │          │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘          │
│                                                            │
│  Crash recovery:                                          │
│  WAL checkpoint → replay committed → discard uncommitted  │
│                                                            │
│  Backup strategy:                                         │
│  [Base backup] + [Archived WAL] → PITR to any moment     │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Write-Ahead Logging is the durability protocol at the heart of PostgreSQL. Before any data page is modified, the database first appends a compact record of the intended change to a sequential log and fsyncs that log to disk. Only after the log is physically durable does the commit return success. The actual data pages are written later by the background checkpointer. This gives durability without the cost of random writes on every commit.

WAL provides three capabilities. Crash recovery: if the server dies, on restart it replays the WAL from the last checkpoint, redoing committed changes and discarding uncommitted ones, so a committed transaction is never lost. Replication: a replica is simply another server replaying the same WAL stream, which is how streaming read replicas stay in sync. And point-in-time recovery: by taking a base backup and continuously archiving every WAL segment, you can restore to any chosen timestamp.

That last capability shapes the entire backup strategy of a banking ledger. A ledger must be auditable and must never lose a committed entry, so the strategy is periodic base backups plus continuous WAL archiving to durable storage like S3. This gives essentially zero committed-data loss and surgical recovery to any moment, not just last night's snapshot.

At the National Bank of India, the ledger ran with synchronous commit so WAL was fsynced before any transfer was acknowledged. WAL was archived continuously to S3 with weekly base backups. When a faulty batch job at 10:00 AM corrupted balances, Pankaj restored the latest base backup and replayed archived WAL to 9:59:59 AM, recovering every good transaction from earlier that morning while excluding the bad batch.

Remember one sentence: log the change durably first and update the data pages after, so a crash is recovered by replaying the log, and a base backup plus archived WAL lets you restore to any moment.
